definition: A nervous or fearful feeling about something that is about to happen.
example: With some trepidation, the first-time hiker stepped onto the swaying rope bridge.
nuance: Trepidation is anxious worry about what lies ahead; it is milder than terror and points toward the future more than plain fear does.
prompt: A student waits backstage before her first piano recital.
options: Waiting for her name to be called, she felt a wave of trepidation in her stomach.
Her trepidation was so complete that she strolled onstage without a single worry.
After months of daily trepidation at the keyboard, she knew every note by heart.
She eyed the plate of cookies set out for intermission with cheerful trepidation.
reasons: A jittery feeling before facing an audience is exactly this kind of anxious anticipation.
Strolling out without any worry describes confidence, the reverse of anxious dread.
This treats the word as if it meant practice or preparation, but it names a feeling.
Looking forward to a treat is pleasure, and a cheerful mood clashes with the word's fearful tone.

practice.prompt: A twelve-year-old is starting at a new school in a different town.
options: At the front office, his mother signed a trepidation form for his class schedule.
The trepidation of seeing his best friend at the bus stop made him smile with relief.
He showed his trepidation by laughing and boasting that nothing about the move scared him.
He walked in on day one with trepidation, unsure anyone would sit with him at lunch.
reasons: This mixes the word up with registration; it names an emotion, not a piece of paperwork.
Relief at a welcome surprise is the opposite of anxious fear about what is coming.
Boasting that nothing is scary shows bravado, not the uneasy fear the word requires.
Worry about an uncertain social situation ahead fits the word's sense of nervous expectation.
